stories.title: Project scaffolding with FastAPI backend and React frontend
stories.description: Initialize the Python project with FastAPI (backend/) and React (frontend/) directory structure. Set up pyproject.toml or requirements.txt with FastAPI, uvicorn, pydantic, anthropic, and httpx as dependencies. Set up frontend with Vite + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS via package.json. Create a Makefile with targets: dev-backend (runs uvicorn on port 8000), dev-frontend (runs Vite dev server on port 3000), and dev (runs both). Implement a health-check endpoint at GET /api/health that returns {"status": "ok"}. Add a .env.example with ANTHROPIC_API_KEY placeholder. Verify: health endpoint returns 200, both servers start without errors, linting passes.

stories.title: Case data models, schemas, and case folder management
stories.description: Define Pydantic models in backend/models/: Case (id, title, facts, claimant_input, respondent_input, status enum [pending, running, completed, escalated], judicial_level, created_at, updated_at), Argument (role, iteration, content, legal_basis, factual_claims, counterarguments, evidence_requests, references, timestamp), CourtEvaluation (consistency_scores, compliance_assessment, adversarial_review, escalation_decision, reasoning_trace), and MCDAResult (criteria_scores, weighted_totals, predicted_winner, confidence). Implement a CaseFolderManager class in backend/services/case_folder.py that creates/loads case directories under data/cases/{case_id}/ with subdirectories: config/, state/, iterations/, outputs/. Each subdirectory stores JSON files. Add unit tests in tests/ for model validation and folder creation/loading.

stories.title: Case intake REST API for external agent submission
stories.description: Implement FastAPI routes in backend/api/cases.py: POST /api/cases accepts a case submission (facts, party_role, supporting_materials) from an external agent, creates a new case with UUID, initializes the case folder via CaseFolderManager, and returns the case ID and status. GET /api/cases/{case_id} retrieves current case state from the case folder. GET /api/cases lists all cases with status. All endpoints return JSON with proper error handling (404 for missing cases, 422 for validation errors). Add integration tests using httpx AsyncClient/TestClient that submit a case, retrieve it, list cases, and verify folder creation and response schemas.

stories.title: Claude API integration layer and base agent abstraction
stories.description: Create a base LLMAgent class in backend/agents/base.py that wraps the Anthropic Python SDK. It should accept a system prompt, conversation history, and optional structured output schema. Call Claude (model configurable, default claude-sonnet-4-20250514) and return parsed output. Include retry logic with exponential backoff, token usage tracking, and configurable temperature. Create a config module in backend/config.py that reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, MODEL_NAME, and other settings from environment variables using pydantic-settings. Write tests in tests/test_agents.py that mock the Anthropic client and verify prompt construction, retry behavior, and response parsing.

stories.title: Claimant and respondent agents with iterative argument loop
stories.description: Implement ClaimantAgent and RespondentAgent in backend/agents/ extending the base LLMAgent. Each agent receives case facts plus the opponent's latest arguments and generates structured arguments (legal_basis, factual_claims, counterarguments, evidence_requests, strategy_notes). Each iteration is persisted to the case folder under iterations/round_{n}_{role}.json. Implement a convergence detector in backend/services/convergence.py that compares consecutive argument versions using structured field diff and similarity scoring to detect when arguments stabilize. Implement an ArgumentLoop orchestrator in backend/services/argument_loop.py that alternates between claimant and respondent until both converge or max_iterations (configurable, default 5) is reached. Write tests with mocked LLM responses verifying iteration files are created, arguments follow the schema, and convergence detection triggers correctly.

stories.title: Legal reference database with precedent retrieval and internet fallback
stories.description: Create a legal reference module in backend/legal_db/. Implement a SQLite-backed store (using aiosqlite or sqlite3) for legal precedents (case_name, jurisdiction, year, summary, full_text, tags, outcome) and laws (code, article, text, jurisdiction). Provide a seed script backend/legal_db/seed.py that loads sample legal data (10-20 representative cases and key statutes). Implement keyword search and TF-IDF based similarity search over the database. Add an internet fallback that uses web search (via httpx) when local DB returns fewer than 3 relevant matches. Expose functions: retrieve_precedents(query, jurisdiction, top_k) and retrieve_laws(topic, jurisdiction). Write tests verifying search returns relevant results from seeded data and fallback triggers when local results are insufficient.

stories.title: Court agent with adversarial internal review and consistency verification
stories.description: Implement CourtAgent in backend/agents/court.py that receives both sides' stable arguments, referenced precedents, and applicable laws. The court agent must: (1) verify internal consistency of each side's arguments and score them, (2) test compliance with applicable laws and flag violations, (3) generate a preliminary judicial conclusion, (4) run an adversarial self-review by generating a counter-opinion challenging its own preliminary conclusion, (5) reconcile the preliminary and counter opinions into a final evaluation, (6) determine whether the case should stay at the current judicial level or escalate. Output is a structured CourtEvaluation written to outputs/court_evaluation.json. The agent must NOT be a simple summarizer -- enforce structured output with separate sections for consistency_analysis, compliance_check, preliminary_opinion, adversarial_challenge, reconciled_decision, and escalation_recommendation. Write tests with mocked responses verifying all sections are populated and the adversarial review actually contains challenges to the preliminary opinion.

stories.title: Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis scoring for case evaluation
stories.description: Implement an MCDA module in backend/evaluation/mcda.py. Define criteria: evidentiary_strength, legal_consistency, procedural_validity, precedent_alignment, appeal_likelihood. Each criterion has a configurable weight (defaults derived from general legal evaluation principles, stored in backend/evaluation/weights.json). The court agent rates each side on each criterion (1-10 scale). Compute weighted scores, normalize to 0-1 range, and determine predicted winner and confidence estimate (based on score differential and criteria agreement across sides). Integrate MCDA into the CourtAgent evaluation pipeline so it runs after the adversarial review. Persist MCDA results to outputs/mcda_scoring.json in the case folder. Write tests verifying score computation, normalization, winner prediction, and confidence estimation with known inputs.

stories.title: Judicial hierarchy model and escalation engine
stories.description: Define a configurable judicial hierarchy in backend/models/hierarchy.py with levels: First Instance, Appeals Court, Superior Court, Supreme Court. Each level has jurisdiction scope, escalation criteria, and procedural requirements stored in a JSON config file backend/config/judicial_hierarchy.json. Implement an EscalationEngine in backend/services/escalation.py that, given a court evaluation, determines if escalation is warranted based on: constitutional questions raised, conflicting precedents detected, procedural irregularities, or explicit escalation recommendation from the court agent. When escalation triggers, update the case judicial_level, archive current level results, and prepare context for re-running the argument loop at the next level with prompts reflecting the higher court's standards and scope. Write tests for escalation trigger logic, hierarchy traversal, and edge cases (already at highest level, no escalation warranted).

stories.title: Full case orchestrator implementing the Ralph Loop pattern
stories.description: Implement CaseOrchestrator in backend/orchestrator.py that ties together the full pipeline: case intake -> claimant/respondent argument iteration -> legal reference retrieval -> court evaluation with adversarial review -> MCDA scoring -> escalation check -> next judicial level loop or final resolution. The orchestrator runs asynchronously using asyncio, updates case status and state files at each phase, and produces the complete final output with all required fields: judicial_stage, arguments_summary, referenced_precedents, referenced_laws, court_evaluation, escalation_decisions, mcda_scoring, predicted_winner, confidence_estimate, and full_reasoning_trace. Implement API endpoints: POST /api/cases/{case_id}/run to trigger orchestration as a background task, GET /api/cases/{case_id}/status for current phase and progress. Write an integration test that runs a full case through the pipeline with mocked LLM calls and verifies all output fields are present.

stories.title: React frontend with case submission form and case list view
stories.description: Build the React frontend in frontend/ with: (1) a case submission page with form fields for case title, facts (textarea), party role (claimant/respondent selector), and supporting materials (text area), with a submit button that POSTs to /api/cases and then navigates to the case detail view; (2) a case list page showing all cases in a table/card layout with columns for ID, title, status badge (color-coded: pending=gray, running=blue, completed=green, escalated=orange), judicial level, and created date; (3) a case detail page showing current state, arguments from each side with iteration history, court evaluation sections, MCDA scores as a comparison table, escalation history, and final outcome. Use React Router for navigation, Tailwind CSS for styling, and fetch/axios for API calls. Configure Vite to proxy /api requests to localhost:8000. Verify: form submits successfully, case list loads and displays correct statuses, detail view renders all sections.

stories.title: Real-time case monitoring dashboard
stories.description: Add a monitoring dashboard page to the React frontend at /monitor. It should show: (1) a summary bar with counts of cases by status (pending, running, completed, escalated), (2) a list of all active/running cases with live status updates via polling every 5 seconds, showing current iteration number, current phase (arguing, evaluating, escalating), and elapsed time, (3) for each case, a collapsible timeline/log view showing each iteration's summary with timestamps, (4) MCDA score progression displayed as a simple comparison view across iterations if multiple judicial levels were evaluated, (5) escalation events highlighted with distinct styling. Backend: add GET /api/cases/{case_id}/timeline endpoint returning the iteration history with timestamps and phase details. Verify: dashboard updates automatically as a case progresses, timeline shows all phases, escalation events are visually distinct.

stories.title: Sample case runner tool for demonstration
stories.description: Create a CLI tool at backend/tools/run_sample.py and expose as POST /api/tools/run-sample. The tool creates a predefined sample case (a contract breach dispute with realistic facts, parties, and supporting details), submits it to the system via the cases API, triggers the orchestrator, and returns the case ID plus a URL to monitor it on the dashboard. Include 2-3 sample case templates as JSON files in backend/tools/sample_cases/ (contract dispute, employment termination, property damage claim). The CLI should work as: python -m backend.tools.run_sample [--template contract|employment|property]. The API endpoint accepts an optional template parameter. Add a 'Run Sample Case' button to the frontend dashboard that calls the API endpoint and navigates to the monitoring view. Write a test verifying the sample case is created, submitted, and the orchestrator is triggered.

stories.title: End-to-end integration tests and project documentation
stories.description: Write end-to-end tests in tests/test_e2e.py that exercise the full flow: submit a case via the API, trigger orchestration, poll until complete, and verify all output fields are present and valid (judicial_stage, arguments, precedents, court_evaluation, escalation_decision, mcda_scoring, predicted_winner, confidence, reasoning_trace). Ensure FastAPI auto-generates OpenAPI/Swagger docs at /docs with descriptions and example payloads for all endpoints. Write a comprehensive README.md covering: project overview, architecture diagram (text-based), setup instructions (Python, Node, env vars), how to run backend and frontend, how external agents interact with the API (with sample curl commands), explanation of the Ralph Loop concept as applied to legal reasoning, description of the judicial hierarchy and MCDA framework, and troubleshooting tips. Verify: all tests pass, /docs endpoint is accessible, README accurately describes the system.

stories.title: Enhanced case detail page with full evaluation data and per-level results
stories.description:
Enhance the React case detail page (frontend/src/pages/CaseDetail.tsx) to display ALL data produced by the orchestration pipeline. Currently the page only shows arguments and basic court evaluation (preliminary opinion, adversarial challenge, reconciled decision). The system produces much more data that is not visible. Changes required:

1. Add new TypeScript interfaces to frontend/src/api.ts: EscalationDecision (should_escalate, reason, current_level, next_level, triggers) and FinalResult (judicial_stage, arguments_summary, referenced_precedents, referenced_laws, court_evaluation, escalation_decisions, mcda_scoring, predicted_winner, confidence_estimate, full_reasoning_trace).

2. Fetch final_result.json in CaseDetail.tsx alongside existing data fetches.

3. Add an Outcome Summary banner at the top (after the header) showing: predicted_winner (styled prominently), confidence_estimate as percentage, and final judicial_stage — sourced from final_result.json.

4. Add a Consistency Scores section showing claimant vs respondent scores from court_evaluation.consistency_scores as a visual comparison (e.g., progress bars or score badges).

5. Add a Compliance Assessment section showing per-party compliance text from court_evaluation.compliance_assessment (claimant and respondent blocks).

6. Enhance the Escalation History section to show structured escalation cards from final_result.escalation_decisions — each card shows: current_level arrow next_level, reason, and trigger list. Style with orange/amber colors. If no escalation, show 'No escalation — resolved at [level]'.

7. Add a Per-Level Evaluation section: when escalation occurred, the system archives prior level results in outputs/level_first_instance/ (etc). Add a backend endpoint GET /api/cases/{case_id}/outputs/level_{slug}/{filename} to serve archived level files. In the frontend, detect archived levels from final_result.escalation_decisions and fetch each level's court_evaluation.json. Display evaluations from each judicial level in collapsible/tabbed sections so the user can compare how different court levels evaluated the case.

8. Add a Referenced Precedents & Laws section showing lists from final_result.referenced_precedents and referenced_laws. If empty, show 'No references found'.

9. Add a Full Reasoning Trace section showing the numbered step-by-step reasoning from final_result.full_reasoning_trace. Style as an ordered list with subtle background.

Section order: Header, Outcome Summary, Case Facts, Arguments, Consistency Scores, Compliance Assessment, Court Evaluation (existing), MCDA Scoring (existing), Escalation History (enhanced), Per-Level Evaluations, Referenced Precedents & Laws, Full Reasoning Trace.

The existing outputs endpoint at GET /api/cases/{case_id}/outputs/{filename} may need to be extended to support nested paths like level_first_instance/court_evaluation.json — check if it already handles subdirectories, and if not, update backend/api/cases.py to support path separators in the filename parameter.

Verify: TypeScript compiles (tsc --noEmit), the detail page renders all new sections with data from the completed Ollama test case, and no regressions in existing tests.

stories.title: Professional courtroom-style UI with animated case progression
stories.description:
Redesign the case detail page and monitoring dashboard into a visually striking, professional courtroom-themed experience with animations that show the legal process unfolding. This is a UI/UX overhaul — no backend changes needed.

1. CASE PROGRESS VISUALIZATION: Create a new CaseProgress component (frontend/src/components/CaseProgress.tsx) that shows the Ralph Loop as a visual pipeline/stepper. Each phase is a node in a horizontal flow: 'Case Filed' -> 'Arguments' -> 'Legal Research' -> 'Court Evaluation' -> 'MCDA Scoring' -> 'Escalation Check' -> 'Resolved'. The active phase should pulse/glow with a subtle animation (CSS @keyframes). Completed phases show a checkmark with a slide-in animation. Future phases are grayed out. If escalation occurs, show a branching arrow looping back to 'Arguments' at the next judicial level with an escalation badge. Use this component at the top of both the case detail page and the monitor page for running cases.

2. ARGUMENT EXCHANGE ANIMATION: On the case detail page, redesign the arguments section to look like a courtroom debate. Show claimant arguments on the left and respondent on the right in a chat/dialogue style layout (similar to a messaging app but formal). Each argument card should animate in with a slide-from-left (claimant) or slide-from-right (respondent) CSS transition when the section first renders or when new arguments arrive during polling. Use a subtle scale-up effect. Claimant side uses deep blue theme, respondent uses deep red/maroon theme. Add a small gavel icon or scales-of-justice icon between the two sides.

3. COURT EVALUATION REVEAL: The court evaluation section should have a dramatic reveal effect. When first loaded or when the user scrolls to it, the preliminary opinion fades in first, then after a brief delay the adversarial challenge slides in from the opposite side (suggesting opposition), then the reconciled decision drops in from above with a gavel-strike visual cue (a brief shake animation or a subtle flash). Use CSS transitions with staggered delays (0ms, 300ms, 600ms). The background should transition from neutral to a warm judicial tone (subtle parchment/cream).

4. MCDA SCORING ANIMATION: Animate the MCDA comparison table so the score bars grow from zero to their final values over 1 second when the section comes into view (use IntersectionObserver for scroll-triggered animation). Show claimant scores as blue bars and respondent as red bars growing side by side for each criterion. The predicted winner should have a trophy or crown icon that scales up with a bounce animation. The confidence percentage should count up from 0% to the final value.

5. LIVE MONITORING ENHANCEMENTS: On the /monitor page, for running cases add a pulsing dot indicator next to the current phase. Add a typewriter-style text effect for the status message (e.g., 'Running argument loop at First Instance...' types out character by character). The elapsed time counter should tick in real-time (update every second, not just on poll). When a case transitions between phases, briefly flash the case card border in gold.

6. OVERALL THEME AND POLISH: Apply a cohesive legal/judicial theme across all pages using Tailwind CSS: dark navy header with gold accents, serif font (Georgia or similar via Tailwind font-family config) for headings and judicial text, clean sans-serif for body text. Add a subtle courthouse/scales icon in the navigation bar next to 'RalphLex'. Add smooth page transitions when navigating between routes (fade-in effect on route change). All animations should respect prefers-reduced-motion media query — disable animations when the user has reduced motion enabled.

7. IMPLEMENTATION NOTES: All animations must be CSS-only (no animation libraries needed). Use Tailwind CSS utility classes where possible, and add custom @keyframes in frontend/src/index.css for complex animations. Use React refs + IntersectionObserver for scroll-triggered animations. For the typewriter effect, a simple useState + setInterval in a custom hook is sufficient. Do NOT install any new npm packages — use only what's already available (React, Tailwind CSS, react-router-dom).

Verify: TypeScript compiles (tsc --noEmit), animations are smooth at 60fps, prefers-reduced-motion disables animations, all existing functionality still works, the UI looks professional and polished on a 1920x1080 screen.

stories.title: Litigation cost and time estimation for each case resolution
stories.description:
Add a litigation cost and time estimation feature that shows parties how much pursuing this case would cost in real US courts, compared to the instant RalphLex resolution. This requires both backend estimation logic and a frontend display component.

BACKEND CHANGES:

1. Create backend/evaluation/cost_estimator.py with a CostEstimator class. It should estimate real-world litigation costs based on: (a) the judicial level reached (First Instance, Appeals, Superior, Supreme Court), (b) the number of argument rounds (proxy for case complexity), (c) case type/category inferred from the facts. Use realistic US litigation cost data:
   - First Instance / Trial Court: $15,000-$75,000 per party in attorney fees, 6-18 months duration, plus $2,000-$10,000 in court filing fees and expert witnesses.
   - Appeals Court: additional $25,000-$100,000 per party, 12-24 months additional.
   - Superior Court / State Supreme: additional $50,000-$200,000 per party, 12-36 months additional.
   - Supreme Court (SCOTUS): additional $200,000-$500,000+ per party, 12-24 months additional.
   Each estimate should include: attorney_fees_per_party (low/high range), court_costs, expert_witness_fees, total_per_party (low/high), total_all_parties (low/high), estimated_duration_months (low/high), and a comparison field showing RalphLex resolution time (computed from case created_at to completed_at) and RalphLex cost ($0 for self-hosted or a nominal API cost estimate based on token usage).

2. The estimator should account for escalation: if the case escalated through multiple levels, the cost is CUMULATIVE (trial + appeal + higher court). Each escalation adds both cost and time. Use the case's actual escalation_decisions list to compute total levels traversed.

3. Add a complexity multiplier based on argument rounds: more rounds = more complex case = higher real-world cost. 1-2 rounds = simple (1.0x), 3-4 rounds = moderate (1.3x), 5+ rounds = complex (1.6x).

4. Integrate the estimator into the orchestrator pipeline: after final resolution (in CaseOrchestrator.run, after saving final_result.json), compute the cost estimate and save it to outputs/cost_estimate.json in the case folder.

5. Add GET /api/cases/{case_id}/outputs/cost_estimate.json support (already handled by the generic outputs endpoint).

FRONTEND CHANGES:

6. Add a CostEstimate TypeScript interface in frontend/src/api.ts with fields matching the backend output.

7. Create a new CostComparison component (frontend/src/components/CostComparison.tsx) that displays:
   - A side-by-side comparison card: 'Traditional Litigation' vs 'RalphLex Resolution'
   - Traditional side shows: attorney fee range per party, court costs, expert fees, total cost range, and estimated time range (e.g., '12-42 months'). Break down by judicial level if escalation occurred (show cumulative cost stacking up per level).
   - RalphLex side shows: actual processing time (from created_at to completed_at, formatted as minutes/seconds), estimated API cost (if using cloud LLM) or '$0 (local LLM)', and a 'savings' calculation showing the cost difference.
   - A prominent 'You saved approximately $X - $Y' banner with the difference.
   - Style with green for savings, use dollar signs and clock icons.

8. Add the CostComparison component to the case detail page (CaseDetail.tsx), positioned after the MCDA Scoring section and before Escalation History. Only show it when the case is completed and cost_estimate.json exists.

Verify: Backend tests for cost estimation logic with known inputs (single level, multi-level escalation, different complexity). TypeScript compiles. The cost comparison renders on the completed test case with realistic numbers. The cumulative cost display is correct for escalated cases.

stories.title: US judicial system showcase sample cases with escalation triggers
stories.description:
Add three new sample case templates designed to showcase the full US judicial escalation system. These cases are crafted with facts that naturally trigger constitutional questions, conflicting precedents, and procedural issues — causing the system to escalate through multiple judicial levels. The templates already exist as JSON files (created manually); this story wires them into the system and ensures they work correctly.

The three new templates are:
- first_amendment: Dr. Elena Vasquez v. State University Board of Regents — a First Amendment retaliation case involving faculty free speech at a public university, with conflicting circuit court precedents (Third vs Ninth Circuit on Garcetti's application to academic speech). Designed to trigger escalation via constitutional questions and conflicting precedents.
- due_process: Maplewood Homeowners Association v. City of Riverside — a Fifth/Fourteenth Amendment case involving regulatory taking through retroactive rezoning under emergency housing statutes, with due process violations. Designed to trigger escalation via constitutional questions (Takings Clause) and procedural irregularities.
- antitrust: United States v. NexaHealth Corp. — a federal antitrust case under the Sherman and Clayton Acts involving PBM market monopolization, with a circuit split on vertical healthcare market analysis standards. Designed to trigger escalation via conflicting precedents and potential Supreme Court review.

Changes required:
1. The JSON template files already exist at backend/tools/sample_cases/first_amendment.json, due_process.json, and antitrust.json. Verify they load correctly via load_template().
2. VALID_TEMPLATES in backend/tools/run_sample.py has already been updated to include the new templates. Verify it matches: ['contract', 'employment', 'property', 'first_amendment', 'due_process', 'antitrust'].
3. The frontend Monitor.tsx template selector has already been updated with the three new options. Verify the options render correctly.
4. Write tests in tests/test_sample_runner.py that verify each new template loads, has required fields (title, facts, party_role), and can be submitted via the API.
5. Update the API tools endpoint validation in backend/api/tools.py to accept the new template names (it uses VALID_TEMPLATES from run_sample.py so this should already work — verify it).

Verify: All three new templates load via load_template(). The template selector shows all 6 options. Tests pass for the new templates. At least one new template can be submitted and triggers orchestration successfully.
